Framlingham
FRAM-ling-um
n. (the Suffolk castle of the Howards where Mary Tudor was proclaimed queen in July 1553)
Old English Framelingaham, the homestead of Framela's people.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Framlingham is the Suffolk market town whose castle, a curtain wall with thirteen towers and no keep, was the seat of the Howard dukes of Norfolk. Its one day of national importance is in July 1553. Edward VI died on the sixth; Northumberland proclaimed Lady Jane Grey; Mary, who had been at Kenninghall, withdrew to Framlingham as the strongest place she could reach and gathered her supporters in the park below the walls. The East Anglian gentry came in, the fleet in Yarmouth roads declared for her, the council in London changed sides, and on the nineteenth she was proclaimed in the City; she rode from Framlingham to London and to a reign in which some three hundred people were burned. The Howards, who had kept the old religion, were restored. The dictionary records the accession as a providence and refuses to make the providence a verdict. That God brought Mary to the throne from a Suffolk castle is certain; that the burnings which followed were therefore approved is not, and the dictionary insists on the distinction because it is the distinction every party in that century got wrong about its own successes.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines providence as the care and superintendence of God; a lot as that which falls by chance; succession as the order of coming into an office; to proclaim as to publish by authority; and a chariot as a car of war.

expand to see more

PROVIDENCE, n. The care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; a manifestation of the care of God.

LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance; the decision of chance or divine providence by casting lots.

SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; the order of coming into a throne or office after another.

PROCLAIM, v.t. To promulgate; to announce; to publish by authority, as a king or a herald.

CHARIOT, n. A half coach; a carriage with four wheels; a car of war used by the ancients in battle.

Key Scripture

Pro 16:33 — "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD."

Psa 146:3 — "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help."

Psa 20:7 — "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God."

Pro 21:31 — "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Suffolk castle of the Howard dukes where Mary Tudor withdrew in July 1553 and was proclaimed queen, going from it to London and to a reign in which some three hundred were burned.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the argument from success, and the dictionary names it as an error committed by every side in the Tudor century. Mary's partisans read her bloodless accession as heaven's endorsement of the old religion and proceeded to the fires; her opponents, when Elizabeth came in, read that as heaven's endorsement of theirs. Both reasoned from an event to a doctrine, which Scripture never permits. That the outcome was God's doing is not in dispute, for “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33); what the outcome does not do is tell anyone what to believe. The rule of faith is the Word, and a providence is not a revelation.

The second paragraph names the practical error that follows, which is the transfer of hope to a person or a party. Framlingham in July 1553 was full of gentlemen calculating which claimant would reward them, and the fleet changed sides on the same arithmetic. The psalmist forbids the whole exercise: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3), and sets the contrast plainly, “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). Solomon grants the duty of preparation and locates the outcome elsewhere, since “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). Mary rode out of a Suffolk park to a crown and to five years; the men who had come in to her park got very little by it, and the three hundred who were burned under her are the dictionary's reason for naming the lesson sharply.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew goral (H1486), a lot; Hebrew nadib-sense of princes in Psalm 146; Hebrew teshu'ah (H8668), safety or deliverance.

expand to see more

Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot, that which is cast or allotted; “The lot is cast into the lap”, Proverbs 16:33.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, decision, the disposing of a matter; “the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD”, Proverbs 16:33.

Hebrew teshu'ah (H8668) — deliverance, safety, salvation; “but safety is of the LORD”, Proverbs 21:31.

Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — a chariot, a team; “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses”, Psalm 20:7.

Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to call to mind; “but we will remember the name of the LORD our God”, Psalm 20:7.

Usage

"“the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33) — the accession of July 1553."

"“Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3) — the gentry calculating in Framlingham park."

"“but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31) — a providence is not a verdict."
